messages.subject: scaling for count regression
parts:
Hello,

As far as I understood sampling works better with the HMC sampling used in  stan if all parameters have roughly the same order of magnitude.
For linear regressions this can be achieved by scaling predictors and criterion to have a zero mean and an sd of 1 (or .5).
As this is not possible for count variables, is the alternative approach to simply add the known mean of the count variable as a constant?

For example, if I want model a count variable "counts" that has a mean of 8
with a design matrix "x" that includes an intercept column.

Instead of using the following in the model block:

beta ~normal(0,1);
phi ~ cauchy(0,2);
eta <- dot_product(x,beta);
counts ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta,phi);

i would calculate 
eta <- dot_product(x,beta) + 8;


does this seem reasonable?

Guido

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling for count regression
parts:
Not necessarily.  There are two factors at work here — the mean
response and the variance of the data.  In most continuous settings
we can rescale the data which corresponds to shifting and scaling
the parameters.  In the discrete case we cannot rescale at all —
an integer divided by a real is not longer an integer, same for
addition/subtraction — and such a transformation wouldn’t have
the same corresponding effect on parameters anyways.  At least
not exactly.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling for count regression
parts:
Yes, you can do that, but I found it didn't make much difference.
We had a discussion here recently of a Poisson with parameters
on the scale of exp(alpha), where alpha is on the order of exp(17 + epsilon).
Unfortunately, taking the parameter to be (17 + epsilon) instead of alpha
didn't help. So it's still an open problem for us.

I'm guessing the problem lies in the derivatives, which are going
to be super-sensitive out in this region due to the exp() scaling.

Of course, in the simple Poisson case, you can just move to a normal
approximation when counts are on the order of 1 billion.

- Bob

I couldn't find what you were referring to in Chapter 6 of Gelman
and Hill. Are you talking about where you mention exposure being
a multiplicative factor?

The formula for the mean of the Poisson we were working with was

for (i in 1:N)
mu[i] <- intercept
+ sigmaMont * varmont[mont[i]]
+ sigmaYear * varyear[year[i]]
+ sigmaERR * inderr[i];

which then feeds into

y ~ poisson_log(mu);

aka

y ~ poisson(exp(mu));

And we expect mu on the scale of 17 here because that's
roughly the mean of the data y. Are you suggesting:

mu[i] <- 17 * (intercept
+ sigmaMont * varmont[mont[i]]
+ sigmaYear * varyear[year[i]]
+ sigmaERR * inderr[i]);

or just

mu[i] <- 17 * intercept
+ sigmaMont * varmont[mont[i]]
+ sigmaYear * varyear[year[i]]
+ sigmaERR * inderr[i];

or something else entirely?

Neither one actually worked with this problem that lme4 can fit
submitted by atzap on the list. At least not in the way I tried it.

- Bob

Thanks everyone for chiming in!

@ Michael: 
I was indeed trying to scale the parameter, not the data. More specifically, 
I was looking for a way to keep all parameters roughly on the same scale,
because my understanding was that this makes it easier to find a good step size 
during adaption of the HMC algorithm. But I am not sure, because my understanding of HMC is superficial.

I agree that the issue I am trying to address is a different thing that what you were thinking about. 
Sorry if my description was unclear.

@ Andrew and Bob:
As Andrew noted, in my initial proposal I did not take
into account that I used neg_binomial_2_log.
I think the log is crucial, and I don't think the last two 
proposals Bob made take this into account.
The first formula of course works, but it could still 
have the problem that the intercept parameter is
orders of magnitude larger than the other parameters.

Here is now one hopefully correct way to set the model up such
that all parameters have a similar order of magnitude:

When I have count data y with a mean of around m
and use a regression approach to calculate log_mu = x*beta,
(where log_mu = log(mean_of_the_Poisson)
and x includes an intercept regressor)

then one would simply write 
y ~ poisson(exp(log_mu) + m)

Does this make sense?

If I remember correctly, it is preferable to use 
y ~ poisson_log(log_mu) instead of y ~ poisson(mu).

But I don't know how to do a simple addition on the log scale.

Please also tell me if it actually does not matter when the parameters 
have different orders of magnitude....

Best - Guido

What Andrew meant by addition on the log-scale is:

y ~ poisson(exp(XB + log(mu_obs)));

Or better:

y ~ poisson_log(XB + log(mu_obs));

XB is the linear predictor, as usual, and log(mu_obs) is the offset, based on the observed data. Basically, the intercept term in XB should now be estimated somewhere close to one because:

lambda = exp(XB + log(mu_obs)) = exp(XB)*exp(log(mu_obs)) = exp(XB) * mu_obs

-Luc
